div.head: Abt 31
div.ab: Gif friman wið fries mannes wif geligeþ, his wergelde abicge 7 oðer wif his agenum scætte begete 7 ðæm oðrum æt þam gebrenge.
Gif friman wið fries mannes wif geligeþ, his wergelde abicge, ⁊ oðer wif his agenum scætte begete ⁊ ðæm oðrum æt ham gebrenge.
Gif friman wið fries mannes wif geligeþ, his wergilde abicge, 7 oðer wif his agenum scætte begete 7 ðæm oðrum æt þam gebrenge.
Wenn ein Freier bei eines freien Mannes Weibe liegt, zahle er [ihm] mit seinem Wergelde und beschaffe ein anderes Weib für sein eigenes Geld und führe es jenem anderen heim.
If a freeman lies with a free man’s wife, let him pay [him] with his wergeld and procure another wife with his own money and bring her home to that other man.
If [one] freeman lies with the wife of [another] freeman, he shall pay [the husband] his [or her] wergeld, and procure a second wife with his own money, and bring her to the other man’s home.
If a freeman lies with the wife of a freeman, he is to atone with his wergild, and to obtain another wife with his own money, and bring her to the other’s home.
If a freeman lies with a free man’s wife, let him buy [him/her] off [with] his/her wergild and obtain another wife [for the husband] [with] his own money and bring her to the other man at home.

note.seg: ham emendiren Price u. folg. Edd.
Price and subsequent editors emend to ham

S. Gl Ehebruch 5c. Diese Art Eherecht ist offenbar noch unbeeinflusst von der Kirche. Doch zeigt zwei Menschenalter später Erzbischof Theodors Bussbuch das Eheband noch unkanonisch locker; ebd., Ehescheidung 3 und: Qui dimiserit uxorem, alteri coniungens se, VII annos poeniteat; qui maculat uxorem proximi, III annos ieiunet; I 14, 8f. — ‘Frei’ wie o. 4¹

See Gl Ehebruch 5c. This kind of marriage law is evidently still uninfluenced by the Church. Yet two generations later Archbishop Theodore's penitential still shows the marriage bond to be uncanonically loose; ibid., Ehescheidung 3, and: Qui dimiserit uxorem, alteri coniungens se, VII annos poeniteat; qui maculat uxorem proximi, III annos ieiunet; I 14, 8f. — ‘Free’ as above 4¹
Dass die Ehefrau gemeint ist, beweist die folgende Zeile
The following line proves that the wedded wife is meant

abycgan nicht ‘erkaufe, kaufe ab’, wozu das Objekt, hier ‘sie’, wie 82 nötig wäre, sondern ‘bezahle, büsse, leiste Genugtuung’ für Missetat. (So jetzt richtig Toller Suppl. Schmid wurde von seiner richtigen Meinung abgelenkt durch Grimm Kl. Schr. V 317f. Vgl. ‘die Falschmünzerei hi ealle abohton durch Erleiden der Verstümmelung’; Ann. Agsax. 1125.) Das Wergeld ist nicht Kaufpreis für die Ehebrecherin, sondern Busse für den Ehebruch. — Der Ehemann war berechtigt zur Ehescheidung. Und dass diese tatsächlich die Regel war, folgt aus dem Gesetz klar. Habicht Verlobung 54 meint, er war nicht zur Scheidung verpflichtet, die sich nur aus Vereinbarung der beiden Männer ergab. Aber das folgt wenigstens nicht aus dem Worte abycgan. Augustins Mitwirken an dem Gesetz widerlegt die von Grimm angenommene Möglichkeit der Bigamie (oðer hiesse dann ‘ein zweites’); die Vertreibung der Ehebrecherin wie zu Tacitus’ Zeit ist für Kent im 7. Jh. bezeugt; s. Gl Ehe 5

abycgan means not ‘purchase, buy off’, which would require an object, here ‘her’, as in 82, but ‘pay for, atone for, give satisfaction’ for an offence. (So now, correctly, Toller Suppl. Schmid was diverted from his correct view by Grimm Kl. Schr. V 317f. Cf. ‘the counterfeiting hi ealle abohton by suffering mutilation’; Ann. Agsax. 1125.) The wergild is not a purchase price for the adulteress but compensation for the adultery. — The husband was entitled to divorce. And the law makes it clear that this was in fact the rule. Habicht Verlobung 54 thinks that he was not obliged to divorce, and that divorce came about only by agreement between the two men. But this at least does not follow from the word abycgan. Augustine's participation in the law refutes the possibility of bigamy assumed by Grimm (oðer would then mean ‘a second’); the expulsion of the adulteress, as in Tacitus’ time, is attested for Kent in the 7th cent.; see Gl Ehe 5

Des Weibes Wergeld verstehen Grimm, Schmid (563 aber zweifelnd), Richthofen (Zur Lex Sax. 305), Weinhold (Deutsche Frauen I 312), Sohm (Trauung 30), Schipper (in Östreich. Rdsch. 1883, 268), Habicht, Rosenthal (Rechtsfolgen des Ehebruchs 55), Moeller (Wergeld des Täters 15. 34). Allerdings bestimmt Baiernrecht: Si quis cum uxore alterius concubuerit libera, . . cum weragildo illius uxoris contra maritum componat; VIII 1. 10. 12; doch ein anderer Text und andere festländische Volksrechte fordern des Ehebrechers Wergeld; Richthofen; Brunner; Sohm Eheschliessung 76. Dies galt um 1100 in England; vgl. Gl Ehebruch 11, ebenso für Raubehe mit der Witwe II Cn 52, für Nonnenschändung Northu 63. Gegen mich führt Brunner Abt 85 an: Ehebruch mit Unfreier büsst deren doppelter Wert (wenn diese seine Auslegung zutrifft); allein die Unfreie kann als Sache gelten. Meine Gegner müssten nachweisen, dass wif dem grammatischen Geschlecht entsprechend weiterhin im Satze als Neutrum behandelt würde; vielmehr verwendet Abt 11. 83 mægdenman, mægðmon (grammatische Masculina) als Feminina, dem natürlichen Geschlechte entsprechend (vgl. Koch Engl. Gram. II § 207); so verfahren Ine 57 und viele andere mit wif; Urk. a. 835 Bi 412; Grein Glossar IV 699; Ælfred Boetius 35, 7

Grimm, Schmid (563, but with doubts), Richthofen (Zur Lex Sax. 305), Weinhold (Deutsche Frauen I 312), Sohm (Trauung 30), Schipper (in Östreich. Rdsch. 1883, 268), Habicht, Rosenthal (Rechtsfolgen des Ehebruchs 55) and Moeller (Wergeld des Täters 15. 34) take this to be the woman's wergild. Bavarian law does indeed lay down: Si quis cum uxore alterius concubuerit libera, . . cum weragildo illius uxoris contra maritum componat; VIII 1. 10. 12; but another text and other continental folk-laws require the adulterer's wergild; Richthofen; Brunner; Sohm Eheschliessung 76. This was the law in England c. 1100; cf. Gl Ehebruch 11; likewise for marriage by abduction of the widow, II Cn 52, and for the violation of nuns, Northu 63. Brunner cites Abt 85 against me: adultery with an unfree woman is compensated with twice her value (if his interpretation is correct); but the unfree woman can be regarded as a thing. My opponents would have to show that wif continues to be treated as a neuter later in the sentence, in accordance with its grammatical gender; on the contrary, Abt 11. 83 uses mægdenman, mægðmon (grammatically masculine) as feminines, in accordance with natural gender (cf. Koch Engl. Gram. II § 207); Ine 57 and many others do the same with wif; charter a. 835 Bi 412; Grein Glossar IV 699; Ælfred Boetius 35, 7
Er bezahle Brautkauf für die zweite Frau
He is to pay the bride-price for the second wife

Für getötete Sklaven, wie für Vieh, fordern Germanische Volksrechte Sklaven gleichen Wertes als Ersatz (Grimm DRA 343). Statt Gleichwertigkeit ist Gefallen des Ehemanns an der gewählten zweiten Frau vorauszusetzen

For slain slaves, as for cattle, Germanic folk-laws demand slaves of equal value as replacement (Grimm DRA 343). Here, instead of equal value, the husband's approval of the second wife chosen is to be presupposed
Vgl. o. 30²
Cf. above 30²
ham (s. d. Wb) zu emendieren empfahl schon Hickes. Durch Ähnlichkeit von þ und h verwechseln Schreiber beide öfter; s. Wb 216 Sp. 2 n. 10. 12
Hickes already recommended emending to ham (see that word in Wb). Because þ and h look alike, scribes often confuse them; see Wb 216 col. 2 n. 10. 12

note.label: ham
note.seg: em. Hickes. þam. H.

The word his is ambiguous. Schmid and other scholars understand the word to refer to the wife’s wergeld, in favour of which may be compared the Lex Baioariorum, cap. viii, 1. 10: Si quis cum uxore alterius concubuerit libera,…cum weragildo illius uxoris contra maritum componat. Liebermann takes his to refer to the wergeld of the adulterer, and urges that otherwise the neuter his would not be used, but the changes of gender in cap. 11 and cap. 83 cited by him are hardly conclusive parallels, since in both cases the pronoun hio occurs in a new sentence. ¶ It would seem that the injured husband in Kent was not difficult to please, unless we are to suppose, with Liebermann, that his consent in regard to the choice of the lady was secured beforehand—but the law, at all events, gives no hint of such a stipulation.

note.label: wergild
note.seg: Grammatically, it is possible that her wergild is meant.

note.label: þam
note.seg: Liebermann suggests emending this to ham, ‘home’; see note f to translation.

note.label: wergild
note.seg: As wif is neuter and the possessive pronoun his can be masculine or neuter, whether the wergild is that of the man or the woman is grammatically ambiguous.

note.label: home.
note.seg: As stated in note c to the Old English text, Liebermann suggests an emendation to ham, ‘home.’ I am not convinced this is necessary. Modern German still retains the idiom ‘bei ihm,’ which is more familiar perhaps in the French ‘chez lui,’ but both instances mean roughly ‘at his home.’ Although we do not find this idiom elsewhere in English, as we have no text that predates this one, I would not rule out the possibility that we are seeing here the remnants of an idiomatic use of the pronoun that does not survive long in the Anglo-Saxon territories. The choice of one interpretation over the other does not materially affect the translation.
